Resolves #22112
Related: #21198, #21603, #22110

Web Desktop explains a refused native popup in the window where the drag started. With pop-ups allowed for the site, a user can drag Mail out, back inside, and out again without releasing the mouse. The second native exit already worked. The new browser regression exercises it under a real per-origin grant with Chrome's normal popup blocker active.

Evidence: L3 (two native browser windows, one held pointer, matched Chrome profiles and an observable refusal on the second exit) → L3 required.

## AC Evidence

| AC | Observed behavior |
| --- | --- |
| AC-1 | In a disposable profile with an explicit grant for the test origin, Mail leaves, returns and leaves again under one press. Releasing outside retains one popup. Back restores the original Mail view, Robin Chen's selected message, dialog and task. The existing two-exit Notes example also covers returning inside before release. |
| AC-2 | Under the default policy, the first popup opens and returns. Chrome declines the next open after consuming activation. The source desktop now displays a non-focusing status and keeps Mail usable. A canceled or stale admission, hidden or closed window, and rejected transport do not display permission guidance. |
| AC-3 | The maintained Web Desktop regression launches Chromium with normal popup blocking. It sends held button movements directly and observes that no fresh activation exists before the second exit in either profile. |

## Deltas from ticket

The matched Web Desktop and Workstation runs established the same origin-permission behavior. The [original Dock decision](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/pull/19539) closes the popup on re-entry. Its [six-crossing journey](https://github.com/neomjs/neo/pull/19546) exercised three native popup generations in one drag. This change keeps that gesture and makes a refused attempt understandable in Web Desktop.

## Contract Ledger

| Surface | Owner and behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `WindowTearOut.open` | Keeps its existing admission / null result. Only a current and visible owner's explicit negative native result calls `owner.onPopupOpenRefused()`. |
| `AppWindow.onPopupOpenRefused` | Presents an eight-second status in the owning app/window. It has no modal surface, moves no focus and asks for no additional activation during the drag. |

## Test Evidence

- On clean `c092605497ef`, the permitted gesture passed. The ordinary-blocking test failed because the desktop displayed no guidance. Both profiles passed with the change.
- A separate production comparison ran Web Desktop Mail and Workstation Audit on the same origin in the same disposable Chrome profile. Both completed the second exit with a grant. With default blocking, both attempted the second open and the browser returned null. A failure reproduced just 596 ms after the first open.
- In an additional production run, Mail and Workstation Audit each completed **three outward and three inward crossings under one press**. Each outward crossing displayed the original content in a distinct native window. Chrome observed activation only on the first open. Mail retained its original dialog, selected message and task, Audit retained its pane, and release left zero popups in both runs.
- The new webdesktop spec attaches a full desktop frame named `desktop-after-refused-tear-out`. Reproduce with `npm run test-e2e -- test/playwright/e2e/webdesktop/RepeatedTearOut.spec.mjs --workers=1`.

Frame critique: the old desktop gave no visual explanation after Mail returned. The candidate shows a three-line status in the upper-right of the 1280 × 800 desktop. The complete message fits, and the original Mail selection and task stay visible.

## Post-Merge Validation

- [ ] Repeat the one-press out → in → out drag with a physical mouse on the merged Web Desktop origin with pop-ups allowed; confirm the same app is under the pointer on the second exit.

### 🧭 Patch-Blind Premise Snapshot

*   **Inputs Read Before Patch:** #22112 (its *Design authority:* line names the 23-11 manual test and the Dock's held-gesture `TearOut.mjs`). The changed-file list. `src/desktop/WindowTearOut.mjs`, `NativeVesselTransaction.openVessel` and `Neo.Main.windowOpen` on `dev`. Workstation's refusal guidance (`VesselWorkspace.POPUP_REFUSAL_MESSAGE`). The October decision trail (#19533 option B).
*   **Expected Solution Shape:** The desktop shows a non-modal, non-focusing notice only when the browser actually refuses the second open, and keeps the app usable on the desktop. Stale or canceled admissions and transport failures stay silent. It must not hardcode refusal detection on activation heuristics. It must not steal focus mid-drag or add a modal. The tests should isolate the outcome classification (unit) from the real per-origin popup policy (browser e2e, granted and blocked profiles).
*   **Patch Verdict:** Matches. `windowOpen` returns `!!window.open(...)`, so `opened === false` is exactly a refusal. `.catch(() => null)` keeps transport errors out of the refusal path. The `me.#entry === entry`, `!entry.retiring` and owner-visibility guards cover stale, canceled and hidden-or-closed cases. `Neo.toast` comes in through `component/Toast.mjs`, which imports `manager/Toast.mjs` where `Neo.toast` is bound.
*   **Premise Coherence:** Coheres with verify-before-assert. The ticket rests on a measured `isActive` flip (true at the first open, false 596 ms later on the second exit), not on the symptom alone. The PR keeps the fail-closed rule of the October decision instead of reopening it.

### 🔬 Depth Floor

**Challenge:** the same browser refusal now has two pieces of guidance at two layers. Workstation's lives in the app (`VesselWorkspace.POPUP_REFUSAL_MESSAGE`, "Allow pop-ups for this site to use multi-window dragging…"). The desktop's lives in the engine family (`AppWindow#onPopupOpenRefused`, "…allow pop-ups for this site and try the drag again."). Product-specific wording is defensible, and nothing breaks today. The day a third product tears out, though, the shared part (detection plus "allow pop-ups for this site") will want one engine-owned home beside `openVessel`, with each product adding its own clause. This is an observation for that day, not a ticket now.

A second, unverified assumption is that Chrome keeps consuming activation on the first `window.open` of a held gesture. The blocked-profile spec asserts that refusal, so a policy change would turn it red loudly instead of letting the notice decay silently.
